The Fe49.6Ni28Al6Ti3Zr0.1C0.2B0.1Cr13 (at.%) MEA samples, labeled as Cr13, were fabricated through arc melting of high-purity raw materials (purity > 99.9 wt%) under a Ti-getter argon atmosphere.
Subsequently, the ingots underwent homogenization at 1100 °C for 2 h, then were rapidly cooled to 25 °C using water.
Afterwards, they were cold-rolled in the longitudinal direction at 25 °C, achieving a total thickness reduction of 85 %.
The cold-rolled sheets were recrystallized at 1100 °C for 30 min and then water quenched to 25 °C (labeled as recrystallized alloys).
Finally, recrystallized sheets were aged at 700 °C for 47 h and then water quenching (labeled as aged alloys).
Besides, parts of recrystallized sheets were aged at 750 °C for up to 5 days to form large precipitates.

TEM image and selected area electron diffraction (SAED) pattern indicate that the spherical L12 nanoprecipitates were evenly dispersed throughout the FCC grain interior, which possess a coherent relationship with the FCC matrix, as supported by the FFT image and inverse FFT (Fig. 1d, d1, e, e1). Corresponding Energy Dispersive Spectroscopy (EDS) maps (Fig. 1d2-d6) show that the FCC matrix is enriched with Cr and Fe, whereas Al, Ni, and Ti are predominant in the L12 precipitates. The mean size and volume fraction of the L12 precipitates are estimated to be ~15 ± 0.4 nm and 28 %, respectively.

The EBSD inverse pole figure (IPF) mapping (Fig. 1b) result reveals a fully recrystallized microstructure characterized by a homogeneous distribution of equiaxed grains with an average size of 29 ± 2 μm (Fig. 1c).
The averaged interspacing of these slip bands was only 0.4 μm at 10 % strains.
Fig. 5a2 shows the formation of thick slip bands characterized by a high dislocation density, along with regions featuring stacking faults (SFs) and low dislocation density between these slip bands.
The interaction among the SFs results in the creation of sessile dislocations, commonly referred to as Lomer–Cottrell locks (L–C locks).

The ongoing multiplication and intersection of planar slip bands lead to a dynamic process of grain subdivision and refinement as deformation occurs (namely Taylor lattices), leading to a significant strain-hardening effect [42].
